resolution.gpt_reasoning: Nevada’s nonpayment-of-rent eviction statute is NRS § 40.253, which requires a written notice demanding either payment of rent or surrender of the premises before the tenant is guilty of unlawful detainer for nonpayment. For residential premises, the current statutory period is 7 judicial days after service of the notice, not 5 days. The 5-day figure appears to reflect an outdated version or a different Nevada eviction notice, while the current nonpayment notice period is 7 judicial days under NRS § 40.253.
resolution.gemini_reasoning: Under NRS § 40.253(1), a tenant who defaults on rent is guilty of unlawful detainer only after being served with a written notice and continuing in possession for 7 judicial days. This statute was amended in 2019, changing the period from 5 days to 7 judicial days, which resolves the conflict between the sources; Source A is outdated, while Source B is correct.
resolution.uncertainty_note: The 7 days are judicial days, so weekends and legal holidays are generally excluded; special rules or additional notice requirements may apply for subsidized housing, lawful rent withholding under NRS § 118A.315, or other statutory exceptions.

flags.gpt_reasoning: Nevada residential pay-or-quit notices are served under NRS 40.280. Subsection (1)(a) covers personal delivery, subsection (1)(b) covers leaving the notice with a suitable person plus mailing, and subsection (1)(c) covers posting/other delivery when no suitable person or ascertainable address is available plus mailing; there is no mail-only method.
flags.gemini_reasoning: Nevada law specifies three methods for serving eviction notices under NRS 40.280(1). Subsection (a) covers personal delivery, (b) covers substituted service (leaving with a suitable person and mailing), and (c) covers posting the notice in a conspicuous place and mailing it when other methods are not possible. The 'current rules file' correctly identified all three valid service methods.

gpt.rationale: For nonpayment of rent by a residential tenant, Nevada requires the landlord to serve a notice requiring the tenant to pay rent or surrender the premises within 7 judicial days after service. The landlord may proceed with eviction only if the tenant fails to comply within that statutory notice period.

federal.name: SCRA § 3951 (Servicemembers Civil Relief Act)
federal.applies_when: Servicemembers and their dependents occupying a residence as their primary dwelling, where the servicemember's military service materially affects their ability to pay the rent.
federal.effect: During a period of military service, a landlord may not evict a servicemember or their dependents from their primary residence without first obtaining a court order. Court may stay proceedings up to 90 days or adjust the rental obligation. Protection applies when monthly rent does not exceed the annual threshold: $4,954.34/month (2024; formula: 130% of BAH for E-5 with dependents, highest BAH area — adjusted annually by DoD). Landlord must file affidavit of non-military-service before default judgment may enter (50 U.S.C. § 3931(b)(1)). FY23 NDAA amendment: replaced CPI-adjusted fixed-dollar threshold with current BAH formula.
